School finances before closure

What happened to the pupil numbers and finances of state schools in the years before they closed, and what that says about early warning for others.

NoteIn short
  • Rolls fall first, and furthest. Of the 241 state primary schools that closed or merged from 2017/18 on, the typical one had lost 13% of its pupils over three years four years before it closed, and 23% by the year before, when it was 63% full against 93% for schools that stayed open.
  • The money follows. Their reserves and in-year balances were close to other schools’ six years out and weakened as the end neared: in the year before closing, 30% were in deficit, against about 9% of open primary schools in a typical year. Income per pupil rose, because a shrinking school keeps its fixed costs and lump sums.
  • There is early warning in schools’ own returns. A simple model of pupils, capacity and finances, trained on closures up to 2020/21, picked out the schools that closed later: the riskiest 5% of returns included 65% of the returns from schools that closed two or three years on. Rolls carry most of the warning; finances add to it.
  • No open school is named here. The page counts schools showing the warning signs by authority. A published list could itself push a school towards closure, as parents and staff read it.

Every state mainstream school that closed with no successor, or merged into another, from 2017/18 to 2025/26 (from Pupil numbers and school places) is followed back through its finance returns: maintained schools’ Consistent Financial Reporting (CFR) from 2014-15 and academies’ accounts returns (AAR) from 2016-17, to 2025-26. A school that became an academy before it closed is followed through both. Each school’s figures are set against all the state schools of its stage still open that year. That is 241 primary and 37 secondary schools; most of what follows is about primary schools, where nearly all closures are.

The years before closure

The order matters. Six years before closure the schools that went on to close were already smaller than most (median percentile 33) and had begun to lose pupils; their finances were near the middle. Rolls kept falling and capacity emptying, year on year; reserves and in-year balances slipped only in the last two or three years. A school’s finances, in other words, mostly record what its rolls have already done: by the time the deficit shows, the pupils have gone.

Secondary closures are few (37 since 2017/18) and more varied, but show the same order: rolls first, then money.

Which signals warn, and how early

A logistic regression asks, for every school-year from 2017-18 to 2023-24, whether the school closed within the next two years, given that year’s return. Each signal’s effect is shown per standard deviation (or yes against no), holding the others fixed.

NoteThe model behind this chart

\[\text{logit}\,\Pr(\text{closes within two years})_{st} = \beta_0 + \sum_j \beta_j x_{jst}\]

for school s in year t, with the signals \(x_j\) as in the chart (a school three years old or more, with at least 10 pupils and a return with income). Percentages are capped (change in pupils at ±50, capacity 20 to 150, reserve ±40, in-year balance ±20) so that a few odd returns cannot steer it.

glm(y ~ log_pupils + chg3 + util_c + res + iy + ipp + area_primary_chg + academy + secondary,
    family = binomial, data = mm)   # 126,199 school-years, 371 closing within two years

The strongest single sign is a falling roll: each standard deviation more of fall over three years more than doubles the odds. An emptier school, a smaller reserve, an in-year deficit, a small school and an area whose primary population is falling all add. Academies are much less likely to close than maintained schools with the same figures. That is partly how the system works rather than how the schools are doing: a struggling academy is more often moved to another trust than closed. Income per pupil goes the other way because, size for size, a school with more per pupil is one that has lost pupils faster than its funding.

Pupil numbers and capacity alone give an AUC of 0.88 on the test years; the finance measures alone 0.86; maintained or academy alone 0.70. Both kinds of signal carry warning, and together they do better than either. Even so, most schools the model flags do not close in the next few years: closure is rare (about 0.3 in 100 school-years), and many schools with the same figures carry on, merge their classes, federate or find pupils.

Simple warning signs

For governors and councils, five signs that can be read straight from a school’s own returns:

A primary school with none of the signs closed within two years in 0.1 cases in 100; with three, 2.7; with four or five, 6.5. The signs pick out a school that needs a conversation about its future, not one that will close.

Where the warning signs are now

Applied to each open school’s latest return (2023-24 to 2025-26), the model puts 865 of 19,427 schools (4.5%) in the band that, over the last seven years, held the riskiest 2% of school-years. That share is higher than 2% because rolls are falling now in more places than they were. The map counts them by authority.

What this cannot tell you

  • Closure is a decision, not a measurement. Councils, dioceses and trusts close schools for many reasons: falling rolls and money, but also buildings, standards, reorganisation (infant and junior schools merging) and local politics. The model describes the schools that were closed, not the ones that should have been.
  • The last year is partly the decision itself. Once closure is proposed, parents move children and rolls fall faster, which is why the early test (two or three years ahead) matters more than the headline one.
  • Academies and maintained schools differ. Academies rarely close: they are moved to another trust. In a multi-academy trust an academy’s reserve is its own share, and the trust’s central reserve can carry it.
  • The returns differ in timing and coverage. CFR years run April to March, AAR years September to August; some schools miss a year; capacity is GIAS’s latest figure, not the figure each year.
  • A warning is not a forecast for one school. Most schools showing the signs do not close in the next few years. That is why no open school is named here.

Data and calculations

Finances. DfE’s Financial Benchmarking and Insights Tool files: CFR full data workbooks for local authority maintained schools, financial years 2014-15 to 2025-26, and AAR downloads for academies, 2016-17 to 2024-25. From each return: pupils (full-time equivalent, including dual registrations where given), total income, total expenditure (as DfE defines them in each year), staff costs and the revenue reserve. The in-year balance is income minus expenditure. Central services rows of multi-academy trusts are left out. A CFR year (April to March) is labelled with the academic year it mostly falls in.

One school, several numbers. A school’s earlier URNs are joined to its latest through GIAS’s one-to-one predecessor links (academy conversion, a change of type), not through mergers. Where a year has two returns (a part-year CFR and an AAR around conversion), the one with the larger income is kept.

Measures. Change in pupils over three years; pupils as a percentage of capacity (GIAS’s latest recorded capacity); revenue reserve and in-year balance as percentages of income; income per pupil; staff costs as a percentage of expenditure. Percentiles are among the state mainstream schools of the same stage still open that year.

Closures. As on Pupil numbers and school places: state mainstream schools closed with no successor or merged, from GIAS, with the last academic year taught. A return for year t counts as “closing within two years” if the school’s last year is t+1 or t+2; returns in or after the last year are left out. The early test uses t+2 or t+3 and leaves out the year before closure.

Current schools. Each open school’s latest return (2023-24 or later), with the model fitted on every year. The highest-risk band is the predicted risk above which the riskiest 2% of school-years from 2017-18 to 2023-24 fall. School-level scores are kept out of the published data.

The code is R/43_finance_closures.R, which writes data/finance_closures.rds.

Adam Dennett · Bartlett Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis, UCL

 

Built from published DfE and Ofsted data. Nothing uses pupil-level records.
